messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 77-year-old software engineer who fled his home country during its civil war. The event that still governs his daily life happened at a military checkpoint: soldiers shouted, “Get down! Hands where I can see them!” He dropped to the ground, and in that frozen moment he saw his wife being pulled aside, a soldier’s rifle butt pressed against her shoulder, a child’s face streaked with tears. Those moments are the only ones he remembers—not a continuous story, but snapshots: the soldier’s boot, the dust, his wife’s eyes. Each snapshot stands alone, a picture he can turn over in his mind without any feeling at all, as if it happened to a stranger. Yet even that emotionless recall carries a strange power: when he looks at those images, he begins to feel detached and unreal, as though the world around him is a film he is not part of.

Kwame rebuilt his life in the United States, eventually retiring from a long career as a software engineer, though he still takes on consulting projects from home. His wife, a quiet woman, now does most of the errands. He has come to believe that going out is dangerous. The trouble began gradually: a neighbor once asked him to move his car—an ordinary instruction—and Kwame felt his chest tighten, his mind filling with the image of a soldier’s raised hand. That command, harmless as it was, brought the whole checkpoint back. He stopped walking the dog. He stopped going to the grocery store. When his wife asks him to take out the trash, he feels the order land like a blow, and he retreats to his home office, pulling up a programming puzzle to keep his mind occupied. The distraction works for a while, but the more he tries to fill every moment with Sudoku or code, the more the snapshots intrude, as if his brain demands attention it cannot have. Sometimes he will be halfway through a puzzle when the picture of his wife being pulled aside flashes in front of him, and then the feeling of unreality descends again.

That feeling itself has become a trigger. When Kwame notices himself beginning to drift, to feel detached from his own living room, it brings the memory roaring back: the dusty smell, the command to get down. And the memory, in turn, makes him more sensitive to any command. After a flashback he will flinch at his wife’s simplest request, certain that being told what to do is the first step toward something worse. So he avoids people entirely. He screens his calls. He has not attended a family gathering in over a year, because the sound of a raised voice—someone calling for attention—instantly transports him to that checkpoint. His avoidance has narrowed his world to the chair in his home office, where he stares at the same puzzle for hours, trying to keep the pictures at bay.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was his wife’s quiet plea. She said she could not watch him disappear any further. He is afraid—afraid that if he speaks about those snapshots they will become real, afraid that the numbness is the only thing protecting him. But he is more afraid of the feeling of unreality, and of the way his own mind keeps replaying the same few moments, each one a picture he cannot close his eyes against.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that the patient's maladaptive strategies (avoidance, distraction) cause or increase triggers; the causal relationship is not conveyed in any paragraph.
